bull_bear.body:
- Funding via bonds/term loans (interest now flowing through P&L post-commissioning). Subansiri ₹27,949 cr revised cost, levelized tariff ~₹7.50/unit (mgmt confident CERC allows full cost as overruns were beyond management control; all PPAs in place).
- Etalin acquisition involves reimbursing SJVN. No dividend specifics discussed on this call.
bull_bear.title: Capital allocation

bull_bear.body:
- **Regulatory/tariff risk:** entire earnings reset hinges on CERC accepting high Subansiri (₹7.50/unit) and Parbati-II revised costs; any disallowance hits returns. Mgmt confident but it is the central swing factor.
- **Geological/execution risk:** Teesta-VI HRT geological issue slowing progress; hydro inherently surprise-prone (mgmt acknowledges "can never avoid a surprise").
- **RE offtake risk:** discoms hesitant to sign standalone-solar PPAs (connectivity only by 2029–30; demand for RTC/solar+wind+battery) — 14,000 MW of bid-out RE remains without PPA.
- **PAF dip:** 9M PAF 79.27%, ~3% below prior-year due to monsoon shutdowns (Dulhasti, Salal, Chamera-I/III).
- **Other-income decline** (lower insurance/business-interruption realisations) is a real headwind to reported numbers.
bull_bear.title: Risks & watch-items

bull_bear.body: - Confident, granular, project-by-project disclosure; CMD repeatedly "100% sure" on PSP offtake and tariff acceptance. Transparent on the 80%-revenue conservatism and willing to quantify (e.g., +₹116 cr to reach adj. PAT, ₹225 cr deferred Parbati-II revenue). PSU optimism but backed by specific physical-progress %s and dates — credible, with usual PSU caveat that timelines historically slip on hydro.
bull_bear.title: Management quality / tone

bull_bear.body:
- **Reported PAT understates run-rate:** 80%-revenue booking + 100% expense recognition on Parbati-II/Subansiri means the earnings inflection is back-loaded to CERC final orders (5–6 months for Parbati-II) — a potential re-rating catalyst rather than current-quarter event.
- **PSP is the strategic pivot:** management explicitly frames PSP/storage as the monetisation of grid solar build-out ("we definitely require storage… 100% sure we can sell").
- **Etalin shifting onto NHPC's balance sheet** materially enlarges the long-term hydro asset base (3,097 MW, India's largest hydro project) — capex commitment but regulated-asset growth.
- **RE PPA bottleneck is sector-wide** (connectivity 2029–30, discoms wanting RTC), not NHPC-specific — affects all REIAs.

bull_bear.body:
- Established track record in developing hydroelectric projects across the country with a competent, experienced workforce skilled in conceptualization, construction, commissioning and operation of hydro projects
- Full capability from concept to commissioning including a full-fledged in-house Design division, giving an edge over other hydro power companies in complex Himalayan environments

bull_bear.title: Bull — competitive strengths

bull_bear.body:
- Geological uncertainties and natural hazards at project sites — Inaccessible terrain, logistics constraints and limits of investigation have serious consequences for execution; tunnelling under high superincumbent cover creates severe stress problems and heavy water ingress. Plants sit in mountainous, geologically active regions exposed to earthquakes, flash floods, landslides, avalanches, Landslide Lake Outburst Floods (LLOF) and Glacial Lake Outburst Floods (GLOF), which can damage infrastructure and cause severe operational disruption.
- Time and cost overruns on hydro construction — Hilly-terrain projects are exposed to landslides, hill-slope collapses, roadblocks, floods and cloud bursts that set back construction schedules; unpredictable geology in long tunnels such as the Head Race Tunnel, and the need to build road tunnels where rock is unstable, add cost. Law and order problems also cause overruns. Volatility in raw material prices and global supply-chain disruption for critical components such as transformers and solar modules are explicitly named as further cost-overrun drivers.
- Long, multi-agency statutory clearance process — Projects require numerous statutory and non-statutory clearances from multiple agencies, organizations and states; the process is complex, tedious and time-consuming and sometimes leads to abnormal delay, affecting project implementation.
- Difficulty securing long-term PPAs and PSAs for new capacity — Beneficiaries prefer short-term purchases through power exchanges or e-procurement over long/medium-term PPAs, while hydro tariffs are relatively high because projects are site-specific with high initial investment. Excessive bidding in the RE sector over the past two years has produced a supply-demand mismatch; delayed connectivity availability and declining tariffs in successive bids make Power Sale Agreements hard to secure, so NHPC faces difficulty dispatching power from new projects under long-term PPAs.
- High initial cost / high tariff and long gestation, with tariff subject to CERC regulation — Hydro development involves long gestation and large initial investment, resulting in high initial tariff. Cash flow and revenue from operations vary with CERC tariff regulations notified from time to time. High initial cost and tariff can be detrimental to obtaining investment sanction and require extensive financial re-engineering and waivers from stakeholders.
- Law & order and security threats; opposition to hydro projects — Projects and power stations located near sensitive border areas and remote locations face law-and-order problems and officials posted there are prone to security threats. Separately, hydroelectric projects face opposition from certain pressure groups, which has created apprehension among developers as some projects get stalled.
- Restrictive state hydro policies and dependence on few contractors — Several state hydro policies require upfront premium and free power over and above mandated free power for project allocation, which CPSEs following Government of India norms find difficult to accept, hampering project acquisition. Separately, very few contractors in India can deliver in remote, difficult-access locations, increasing dependence on a limited contractor pool.
- Climate change (BRSR material issue, rated Risk with negative financial implication) — Extreme weather events - floods, reduced river flows - may disrupt operations and in extreme cases damage infrastructure, raising restoration costs. Mitigation cited: GLOF and LLOF studies and Early Warning Systems at all hydro projects in operation and under implementation established as an integrated hazard monitoring, forecasting and prediction system, plus emission reduction (e-vehicles, green hydrogen) and energy conservation measures.
- Business concentration in a single activity and hydrology-dependent output — 94.18% of turnover comes from power generation by hydro-electric power plants (wind 0.13%, solar 0.35%, trading 0.17%, consultancy 0.50%), and generation is subject to the inherent hydrology-related variability of river flows. [Provenance: the turnover-mix percentages appear in BRSR Section A items 16-17, which arrived in the SIBLING profile/governance/registry bundles; the routed risks_esg BRSR extract begins after that table. Included here because concentration is a structural risk even though the AR does not label it one.]
- Other BRSR material issues rated as Risk: biodiversity conservation, safety & working conditions, and compliance — Biodiversity - impacts of submergence areas require EIA-based, third-party-assessed project-specific Environmental Management Plans implemented with state government departments. Safety - construction and operation require strict safety adherence; failure impedes productivity and causes financial and reputational loss, mitigated through the Safety Policy, training, audits, monitoring and mock drills. Compliance - non-compliance can lead to legal penalties, operational disruption and reputational damage; all requisite statutory clearances are taken before construction starts and periodic compliance reports are filed. All three are rated as having negative financial implications.

latest_quarter.body:
- **vs Q2 FY26 / prior calls:** Subansiri Lower moved from construction to commissioning (2 units COD'd, 3rd this week, 4th by Mar'26) — the headline change.
- Dibang dam package: previously the lone pending tender; price bid **now opened**, award expected this month — pipeline de-risking.
- Karnisar 300 MW solar **fully commissioned** (now NHPC's largest operational solar) vs under-construction earlier.
- Etalin (3,097 MW) **confirmed onto NHPC balance sheet** (transferred from SJVN) — new addition to disclosed pipeline.
- New explicit capex glide path articulated: FY26 ₹13,300 cr → FY27 ₹15,000 cr → ₹12–13k cr/yr.
- PSP pipeline crystallised into named projects (Omkareshwar, Savitri, Kalu, Masinta) with CY26 start commitment.
- Q3 revenue dipped 3% YoY purely on prior-year ~₹500 cr one-off base; generation up 23% YoY signals underlying momentum.

outlook.title: Growth verticals / optionality

outlook.body:
- Diversify beyond hydropower into solar, wind, pumped storage and green hydrogen to become a fully diversified green energy major / integrated clean energy company, while retaining hydropower as the core
- Build a pipeline of Pumped Storage Projects (PSPs) as the storage backbone of the grid, positioning hydro as the natural complement to India's expanding solar and wind capacity
- Scale up capital expenditure to execute the large project pipeline while maintaining a prudent capital structure, funded through a balanced mix of internal accruals, government support and debt financing
- Finance new hydro projects at a debt:equity ratio generally of 70:30 and solar/wind projects largely at 80:20, using the highest domestic credit rating and low-geared capital structure to raise debt for capex
- Monetize free cash components of operating stations under the National Monetization Pipeline (Return on Equity of Chamera-III and Parbati-III monetized for the next 10 years)
- Expand internationally, principally in Nepal, under the Government of India directive for CPSEs to strengthen footprints in neighbouring countries and evolve into globally recognized multinational enterprises
- Pursue joint-venture arrangements and power purchase agreements in Nepal with a development framework covering both domestic supply and cross-border electricity exports
- Develop pumped storage and renewable projects jointly with state governments through MoUs and JV vehicles (e.g. APGENCO NHPC Green Energy Limited)
- Grow the consultancy business by sharing hydropower best practices with organisations in India and neighbouring countries
- Treat Information Technology as a strategic tool: implement New Age ERP (SAP S/4 HANA) across core business areas, with Business Continuity and Disaster Recovery plans in place
- Maintain the Green Credit Programme and environmental commitments (EIA/EMP at every project, Early Warning Systems at all power stations/projects, catchment area treatment, biodiversity conservation, R&R of project-affected families)
- NHPC states a consistent track record of dividend payment, paying an interim dividend during the year and recommending a final dividend for Board/AGM approval; for FY 2025-26 an interim dividend of 14.00% (Rs 1.40 per equity share) was paid in February 2026 and a final dividend of 2.10% (Rs 0.21 per equity share) has been recommended, to be paid out of the profits of the year. As a CPSE, a cash contribution is made to the Government of India's exchequer through dividend. Company policy is to fund growth through a balanced mix of internal accruals, government support and debt financing while maintaining a prudent capital structure as capital expenditure scales up, with new hydro projects generally financed at a 70:30 debt-equity ratio and solar/wind projects largely at 80:20; the equity component is to be met from internal resources, and a low-geared capital structure plus the highest domestic credit rating ('AAA' stable) and an international rating at par with sovereign ('Baa3' stable) are cited as enabling debt raising for capex. The Company also monetizes free cash components of operating stations under the National Monetization Pipeline. During 2025-26 the Company did not transfer any amount to any reserve. Full compliance is maintained with Debenture Trust Deed covenants, with security cover consistently well above the regulatory threshold and no instance of default on any loan or debt obligation. [Provenance: the dividend percentages come from the Notice of AGM in this bundle; the funding-mix, debt-equity ratio, credit-rating, monetization, reserve-transfer and covenant statements come from the Chairman's Statement and Directors' Report text that arrived in the SIBLING strategy_outlook and profile bundles, not in this bundle. No profit, revenue or balance-sheet figures are reproduced.]
- Capacity transition targets (BRSR Principle 2 and 6): install 3,000 MW hydro and 1,200 MW other renewable energy capacity by 2030; achieve 38,500 MW by FY 2033-34; become a 50,000 MW company by 2047. Reported progress: 1550 MW hydro (Parbati-II 800 MW, Subansiri Lower 750 MW) and 300 MW solar added in FY 2025-26, with 9,454 MW across 16 RE projects under construction. [Provenance: BRSR Principle target/performance tables arrived in the SIBLING capex_expansion bundle.]
- 'Zero Accident' and 'Zero Fatality' workplace - an ongoing target with continuous monitoring; zero fatalities achieved for the third consecutive year. [Sibling capex_expansion bundle.]
- Carbon reduction through EV adoption and DG-set retrofitting; renewable energy consumption as a share of total energy consumption increased to 79.4% from 73.7% in the previous year; 1850 MW of RE capacity added during the year. [Sibling capex_expansion bundle.]
- 100% sustainable sourcing and preferential procurement from Micro and Small Enterprises: in FY 2025-26 NHPC (standalone) procured 60.73% of total annual procurement from MSEs against a 25% mandate, including 5.49% from SC/ST-owned MSEs (against a 4% sub-target) and 4.60% from women-owned MSEs (against a 3% sub-target); 2,594 MSEs benefited, of which 189 were SC/ST-owned and 573 women-owned.
- Zero pending stakeholder grievances at year-end, monitored annually - 100% of grievances resolved through CPGRAMS; FY 2025-26 complaints closed with nil pending for communities (200 filed), investors other than shareholders (44), shareholders (74), employees and workers (4) and customers (0), with 1 of 11 value-chain-partner complaints pending and stated to be resolved in FY 2026-27.
- Board-level Risk Management Committee plus a Risk Assessment Committee under a Chief Risk Officer, operating a Risk Management Policy in force since 2009 (revisions in 2015, 2022 and 2024); 70 key risks currently identified, up from an initial 54.
- Climate resilience infrastructure: Early Warning Systems installed or under progress at all power stations/projects to receive early warnings from upstream, with hooters and caution boards at dams and power houses to alert downstream populations before water release; GLOF and LLOF studies at all hydro projects. [EWS/hooters detail from the sibling strategy_outlook bundle.]
- Environmental management embedded in the project cycle: EIA studies at investigation stage, Environmental Management Plans formulated and implemented, compliance with OHSAS safety systems and environmental laws regularly monitored; catchment area treatment and biodiversity conservation.
- Green Credit Programme participation since August 2024 - 25 plantation blocks covering 224 hectares in Gujarat (170 hectares plantable), Rs 1,551.47 lakh remitted to ICFRE Dehradun, against which Utilization Certificates of Rs 914.63 lakh have been submitted for expenditure to March 31, 2025; monitoring jointly by ICFRE, NHPC and the Gujarat Forest Department. [Sibling strategy_outlook bundle.]
- Rehabilitation & Resettlement: R&R Plans for Project Affected Families under the Right to Fair Compensation and Transparency in Land Acquisition, Rehabilitation and Resettlement Act, 2013, a policy reserving certain works through competitive bidding for PAFs and local people near projects, and skill development training for PAFs and locals.
- Human rights and diversity: no human rights violations reported during the year; female participation stands at 10% among employees and 12% among workers; workforce diversity and inclusion maintained at all levels. [Sibling capex_expansion bundle.]
- Ethics and governance framework: Code of Business Conduct and Ethics, Whistle Blower Policy and structured related-party-transaction procedures; no cases of bribery and corruption reported during the period; independent Vigilance Department headed by a Chief Vigilance Officer appointed by the Government of India, with BIS surveillance audit of vigilance processes concluded satisfactorily.
- BRSR oversight vested in Mr. Mahesh Kumar Sharma, Director (Finance) (DIN 11306355), as the highest authority responsible for implementation and oversight of the Business Responsibility policies. [Sibling capex_expansion bundle.]
- Transparency: RTI Act implemented with designated Appellate Authority, CPIO and APIOs at all locations - in FY 2025-26, 796 applications and 66 first-stage appeals received, with 792 (99.50%) applications and 66 (100%) appeals disposed, and all 8 second-stage appeals before the CIC disposed in NHPC's favour.
outlook.title: Strategy & capital allocation

outlook.body: NHPC is executing a large multi-technology expansion programme. On hydro, the group had 17 projects aggregating 9204 MW under construction and added a record 1850 MW in FY 2025-26 (Subansiri Lower 750 MW, Parbati-II 800 MW, Karnisar Solar 300 MW). On renewables, commissioned RE plants (including subsidiary companies) total 565.78 MW - 50 MW wind at Jaisalmer, 50 MW solar at Theni & Dindigul, the 300 MW Karnisar solar plant at Bikaner (COD of full capacity declared w.e.f. October 16, 2025), 0.7 MW at Central University Ajmer via NHPC REL, 65 MW at Kalpi via BSUL, 88 MW Omkareshwar floating solar and 8 MW Sanchi solar via NHDC, and 4.08 MW rooftop solar. As a developer NHPC is implementing 1197.68 MW of RE projects on EPC mode: 600 MW Kutch (Gujarat) and 100 MW N.P. Kunta (Andhra Pradesh) under the CPSU Scheme, 200 MW each at GSECL Solar Park Khavda Stage-1 and Stage-3 (Gujarat) under TBCB, 50 MW floating solar at West Kallada (Kerala), 40 MW at Ganjam (Odisha) and 7.68 MW rooftop under PM Surya Ghar. Stated timelines: N.P. Kunta targeted for Q2 FY 2026-27 and Kutch for Q4 FY 2026-27; both Khavda TBCB projects anticipated in Q2 FY 2026-27 subject to transmission connectivity; West Kallada and Ganjam targeted during FY 2026-27. Beyond its own balance sheet, NHPC acts as a Renewable Energy Implementing Agency (REIA) with 6278 MW under construction (649 MW Phase-I, 5129 MW under the MNRE FY2023-24 bidding calendar, 500 MW FDRE under FY2024-25) and 1570 MW already commissioned through developers in Rajasthan; a further 12832 MW awaits PSA/PPA signing (1812 MW from FY2023-24 and 11020 MW from FY2024-25). Under Phase-I NHPC awarded 2000 MW of solar of which 1351 MW is commissioned/partially commissioned, 349 MW is expected in FY 2026-27 and 300 MW is held up on GIB and connectivity issues (sub-judice before CERC). As a BESS Implementing Agency, NHPC has awarded the entire 1500 MWh allocated under the VGF scheme - 500 MWh in Kerala at 4 locations (single-cycle 4-hour) and 1000 MWh in Andhra Pradesh at 3 locations (two-cycle 2-hour) - all expected to be commissioned during FY 2026-27. Subsidiary BSUL is implementing a 1200 MW Solar Park at Jalaun, Uttar Pradesh and a 45 MW solar project at Madhogarh; 95.26 MW of rooftop solar is in various stages (2.78 MW own stations/offices, 67.53 MW allocated States/UTs, 24.95 MW Central Ministries) with five States/UTs (Haryana, J&K, Sikkim, Manipur, Nagaland) and eight Central Ministries assigned under PM Surya Ghar. A 25 kWe pilot Green Hydrogen project at Leh and a pilot green hydrogen-based e-mobility project at Chamba (Himachal Pradesh) are in advanced stages of implementation. BRSR-stated capacity goals: install 3,000 MW hydro and 1,200 MW other renewable capacity by 2030, achieve 38,500 MW by FY 2033-34 and become a 50,000 MW company by 2047; against these, 9,454 MW across 16 RE projects (10 hydro, 6 solar) is reported under construction.
outlook.title: Capex & expansion plans

outlook.body:
- India's commitment to 500 GW of non-fossil fuel capacity by 2030 and Net-Zero emissions by 2070 places renewable and hydro power at the centre of the country's energy strategy
- Rising electricity demand driven by industrialisation, electrification of mobility and data-centre growth
- Hydropower is being recognised afresh for grid balancing, peaking support and round-the-clock storage through pumped storage projects
- Government initiatives creating a conducive environment for capacity addition: Hydro Purchase Obligation, tariff rationalisation for legacy projects, budgetary support for enabling infrastructure in Himalayan and North-Eastern States, and renewed thrust on PSPs
- Generation is subject to inherent hydrology-related variability of river flows; operations focus on plant availability, efficient reservoir management and preventive maintenance
- For new project financing, CERC Regulations govern the debt-equity structure; NHPC states it has sufficient internal resources for the equity component of future capex targets
- Credit standing as a driver of funding cost and access: highest domestic rating 'AAA' (stable) from ICRA, CARE and India Ratings, and international rating 'Baa3' (stable) from Moody's, at par with sovereign
- Consolidated installed capacity, together with subsidiaries and joint ventures, crossed 9333 MW from 31 power stations, with a further 17 projects aggregating 9204 MW under construction
- CVPPL (58.16% NHPC / 41.84% JKSPDCL) is developing four hydro-electric projects in the UT of Jammu & Kashmir: Pakal Dul HE Project (1000 MW), Kiru HE Project (624 MW), Kwar HE Project (540 MW) and Kirthai-II HE Project (820 MW)
- ANGEL (50:50 NHPC-APGENCO JV) is pursuing three projects aggregating 3270 MW: Gadikota (1200 MW), Aravetipalli (1320 MW) and Deenepalli (750 MW)
- Nepal: NHPC is associated with three hydropower projects - West Seti (800 MW), Seti River-6 (460 MW) and Phukot Karnali (624 MW); DPRs for West Seti and Seti River-6 submitted to Investment Board Nepal, technical clearance to the Final DPR of West Seti accorded by IBN in August 2025; Inception Report and DPR Review Report for Phukot Karnali submitted to VUCL, Nepal
- NHDC operates two hydro power stations - Indira Sagar (1000 MW) and Omkareshwar (520 MW) - plus 8 MW Sanchi Solar and 88 MW Omkareshwar Floating Solar in Madhya Pradesh
- Consultancy: revenue of Rs 51.04 crore generated through consultancy services during FY 2025-26 (stated verbatim in the Directors' Report consultancy section)
- Already commissioned on deposit basis abroad: 14.1 MW Devighat Hydropower Project in Nepal and 60 MW Kurichu Hydropower Project in Bhutan; footprints marked in Nepal, Bhutan, Myanmar, Tajikistan, Nigeria and Ethiopia

risks.note: Inaccessible terrain, logistics constraints and limits of investigation have serious consequences for execution; tunnelling under high superincumbent cover creates severe stress problems and heavy water ingress. Plants sit in mountainous, geologically active regions exposed to earthquakes, flash floods, landslides, avalanches, Landslide Lake Outburst Floods (LLOF) and Glacial Lake Outburst Floods (GLOF), which can damage infrastructure and cause severe operational disruption.
risks.risk: Geological uncertainties and natural hazards at project sites

risks.note: Hilly-terrain projects are exposed to landslides, hill-slope collapses, roadblocks, floods and cloud bursts that set back construction schedules; unpredictable geology in long tunnels such as the Head Race Tunnel, and the need to build road tunnels where rock is unstable, add cost. Law and order problems also cause overruns. Volatility in raw material prices and global supply-chain disruption for critical components such as transformers and solar modules are explicitly named as further cost-overrun drivers.
risks.risk: Time and cost overruns on hydro construction

risks.note: Projects require numerous statutory and non-statutory clearances from multiple agencies, organizations and states; the process is complex, tedious and time-consuming and sometimes leads to abnormal delay, affecting project implementation.

Beneficiaries prefer short-term purchases through power exchanges or e-procurement over long/medium-term PPAs, while hydro tariffs are relatively high because projects are site-specific with high initial investment. Excessive bidding in the RE sector over the past two years has produced a supply-demand mismatch; delayed connectivity availability and declining tariffs in successive bids make Power Sale Agreements hard to secure, so NHPC faces difficulty dispatching power from new projects under long-term PPAs.
risks.risk: Difficulty securing long-term PPAs and PSAs for new capacity

risks.note: Hydro development involves long gestation and large initial investment, resulting in high initial tariff. Cash flow and revenue from operations vary with CERC tariff regulations notified from time to time. High initial cost and tariff can be detrimental to obtaining investment sanction and require extensive financial re-engineering and waivers from stakeholders.
risks.risk: High initial cost / high tariff and long gestation, with tariff subject to CERC regulation

risks.note: Projects and power stations located near sensitive border areas and remote locations face law-and-order problems and officials posted there are prone to security threats. Separately, hydroelectric projects face opposition from certain pressure groups, which has created apprehension among developers as some projects get stalled.
risks.risk: Law & order and security threats; opposition to hydro projects

risks.note: Several state hydro policies require upfront premium and free power over and above mandated free power for project allocation, which CPSEs following Government of India norms find difficult to accept, hampering project acquisition. Separately, very few contractors in India can deliver in remote, difficult-access locations, increasing dependence on a limited contractor pool.
risks.risk: Restrictive state hydro policies and dependence on few contractors

risks.note: Extreme weather events - floods, reduced river flows - may disrupt operations and in extreme cases damage infrastructure, raising restoration costs. Mitigation cited: GLOF and LLOF studies and Early Warning Systems at all hydro projects in operation and under implementation established as an integrated hazard monitoring, forecasting and prediction system, plus emission reduction (e-vehicles, green hydrogen) and energy conservation measures.
risks.risk: Climate change (BRSR material issue, rated Risk with negative financial implication)
